CHART CODE
 import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

years = [1995, 1997, 1999, 2001, 2003, 2005, 2007, 2009]
brazil_income_share = [17.2, 16.8, 17.3, 17.5, 17.6, 17.8, 18.1, 17.9]
ecuador_income_share = [19.0, 19.5, 17.5, 18.0, 18.5, 18.6, 19.2, 18.8]
chile_income_share = [16.5, 16.2, 16.0, 16.3, 16.7, 16.9, 17.2, 17.0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 7))

markerline_brazil, stemline_brazil, baseline_brazil = ax.stem(
    years, brazil_income_share, linefmt='-', markerfmt='o', basefmt=" ", label='Ecuador'
)
markerline_ecuador, stemline_ecuador, baseline_ecuador = ax.stem(
    years, ecuador_income_share, linefmt='-', markerfmt='s', basefmt=" ", label='Brazil'
)
markerline_chile, stemline_chile, baseline_chile = ax.stem(
    years, chile_income_share, linefmt='-', markerfmt='^', basefmt=" ", label='Chile'
)

plt.setp(markerline_brazil, markersize=8, color='#2E86C1')
plt.setp(stemline_brazil, color='#2E86C1', linewidth=2)
plt.setp(markerline_ecuador, markersize=8, color='#E74C3C')
plt.setp(stemline_ecuador, color='#E74C3C', linewidth=2)
plt.setp(markerline_chile, markersize=8, color='#27AE60')
plt.setp(stemline_chile, color='#27AE60', linewidth=2)

ax.set_xlabel('Year')
ax.set_ylabel('Population share (%)')
ax.set_title('Income Share Held by Bottom 20% of Population in South America (1995-2009)')
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.set_ylim(14, 21)
ax.legend()
ax.grid(axis='y', linestyle='--', alpha=0.7)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.gca().set_ylim(14, 19.35)
plt.savefig('output.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
SUMMARY
 This image is a stem plot that illustrates the income share held by the bottom 20% of the population in three South American countries—Brazil, Ecuador, and Chile—over the period from 1995 to 2009. The chart features three distinct data series, each represented with unique colors and markers: Brazil in blue with circular markers, Ecuador in red with square markers, and Chile in green with triangular markers.

The x-axis represents the years at two-year intervals from 1995 to 2009, while the y-axis indicates the income share held in percentage, ranging from 14% to 21%. Each data point is connected to the baseline by a vertical line, creating a stem-like appearance.

In 1995, Brazil's income share starts at 17.2%, dips slightly to 16.8% in 1997, and then experiences a gradual increase, peaking at 18.1% in 2007 before slightly decreasing to 17.9% in 2009. Ecuador exhibits more fluctuation, beginning at 19.0% in 1995, rising to 19.5% in 1997, then dropping significantly to 17.5% in 1999. It subsequently increases to 18.0% in 2001, 18.5% in 2003, 18.6% in 2005, and peaks at 19.2% in 2007 before falling to 18.8% in 2009. Chile's income share shows a more stable pattern, starting at 16.5% in 1995, decreasing to 16.2% in 1997, and then hovering around 16.0% to 16.3% until 2001. It gradually rises to 16.7% in 2003, 16.9% in 2005, peaking at 17.2% in 2007, and slightly declining to 17.0% in 2009.

The chart provides a clear comparison of how the income share for the bottom 20% of the population has evolved in these countries over the 14-year span, highlighting both the fluctuations and trends within each nation.

p.write_text(s)
exec(compile(s, "chart.py", "exec"))

import numpy as np
data = pd.read_csv("table.csv")
for name, marker in [("Brazil", markerline_brazil), ("Ecuador", markerline_ecuador), ("Chile", markerline_chile)]:
    assert np.array_equal(marker.get_xdata(), data["year"].to_numpy())
    assert np.allclose(marker.get_ydata(), data[name].to_numpy())
    print(name, "data verified; color:", marker.get_color(), "marker:", marker.get_marker())
